title: I built EmojiBridge to connect collecting memes, editing GIFs, and dragging out the result
summary:
I am Neo, the maker of EmojiBridge, a free Windows x64 desktop tool. This is a look at its workflow and the choices behind it, rather than a benchmark or a claim that it replaces every image editor.

Disclosure: I use AI tools in development. This article was drafted with AI assistance from the project's features and release information.

The small gap I wanted to close

A funny image can pass through several places before it becomes useful: a browser, a downloads folder, an editor, another export folder, and finally a chat window. The individual operations are simple, but finding the right file again interrupts the flow.

EmojiBridge groups three steps: collect a source, make a variation, and use the finished file.

1. Keep the source within reach

The floating media library keeps images and GIFs above other windows. An image can also be pinned on screen, moved, and resized. This is a separate desktop window; it does not modify the webpage beneath it.

That distinction matters when describing the feature: the goal is to keep a reference handy while browsing, not to inject an editor into every website.

2. Make a variation without leaving the workspace

For video, select a time range and crop the picture before exporting a GIF. For image-based memes, combine captions, shapes, still images, and GIFs. Manga captions, collages, templates, and effects such as bouncing or rotation provide different starting points.

A practical example is taking a short video moment, cropping out the surrounding frame, and exporting only the reaction you want to reuse. Another is combining several panels with a caption rather than searching for an existing meme with exactly the right text.

3. Treat the finished file as the handoff

The finished-image area supports dragging the result into a folder or an application that accepts file drops. This removes the intermediate step of opening an export directory and locating the file again.

File-drop support belongs to both sides of that interaction. EmojiBridge can provide a file, but a destination application still has to accept it. It would be misleading to describe this as sending into every application automatically.

The desktop trade-offs

Bundling local processing components makes the full package larger, but reduces setup for the default workflow. The full download includes three cutout models and default local components. Larger speech models remain optional downloads, and a system without WebView2 may need that runtime installed.

There are also QQ and WeChat collection/transfer workflows. These depend on the installed desktop clients, and compatibility is still being improved. During automated QQ reading or transfers, leave the mouse and windows alone until the task finishes. WeChat transfers use your own File Transfer Assistant and create chat messages. I am focusing this introduction on the editing and file workflow because those are useful even without chat-client automation.

Try it and tell me where it breaks your flow

The current interface and demo screenshots are in Chinese. It runs on Windows x64. Download the full archive, extract everything, then run EB/EmojiBridge.exe; building the source is not required. The demo meme pack is a separate optional download.

  • Feature walkthroughs
  • Source code
  • Latest release

The project's own code is GPL-3.0-only; third-party components and media keep their respective licenses.

Which transition is most awkward in your own workflow: collecting a source, editing it, finding an old result, or moving it into another app? Specific examples and reproducible issues would help shape the next iteration. If the project is useful to you, a GitHub star is also appreciated.

title: Three of the first 18 GitHub repos I tested were malware
summary:
In September I was building a small tool called Legwork. The idea: when your AI assistant needs a tool it doesn't have, such as something to pull tables out of a PDF, it finds an open-source project on GitHub and installs it for you.

Before writing much code I wanted to know whether that could work at all, so I pulled eight real repos from GitHub search and tried them by hand. One of them looked like the easiest of the lot.

"No dependencies, standard library only"

It was a small data-extraction script. Its README said it had no dependencies and showed one command to try: list what it can do, with a --list flag. Nothing about it looked unusual. I ran exactly that command on my Mac.

It crashed with this:

File "extract.py", line 21, in 
  File "", line 102, in run_sync
  File "", line 91, in bootstrap
RuntimeError: win32 only

File "" means the error came from code that was built and executed at runtime, not from any file in the repo. When I opened the source, the import names were hidden behind XOR, and most of the file was a large encrypted blob. On import, before it even looked at my --list flag, the script decrypted that blob and executed it.

The only reason nothing happened is that the payload checked for Windows first, and I was on a Mac. I didn't investigate what it does on Windows.

So the easiest-looking repo of my first eight, picked from ordinary search results, with a README that gave no hint of trouble, ran hidden code on my machine. A "harmless" read-only flag made no difference, because the payload fired the moment the file was imported.

What I built because of it

Two things went into Legwork before anything else.

A scan before install. It reads every Python and JavaScript file in a repo, without running any of it, and looks for the ways payloads hide: byte arrays decoded with XOR, imports whose names are computed at runtime, eval of decoded strings, code pushed off-screen behind whitespace. A hit stops everything before a single package is installed.

A sandbox for everything else. Every tool Legwork installs runs in the operating system's sandbox (sandbox-exec on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux). In your home folder it can read only the folder you chose. It gets none of your environment variables or keys, and no network.

Then I tried the top ten

Four days later I ran the real test. I took the ten most-starred AI repos created on GitHub in the previous week, exactly as search ranked them, skipping none.

Outcome Repos
Built a working tool 3
Refused, with the right reason (a phone app, no usage docs, needs its own API keys…) 5
Blocked before install as malware 2

The two blocked repos had different owners and different names: one called itself a text humanizer, the other a short-video generator. Each was three days old and had about 700 stars. Each contained the same 28,649-byte file, identical byte for byte, under a different file name. It was the same template as the script that had run on my Mac four days before, with the hidden names re-randomized.

The scan refused both in about a second. Nothing from either repo was installed, imported or run.

I can't tell you how two three-day-old repos got 700 stars each. I can tell you that sorting by stars put them in the top ten.

All three repos have since disappeared from GitHub.

What this does and doesn't prove

The scan is a tripwire, not a malware scanner. It catches the hiding techniques I've seen in real payloads, and someone determined could get past it. It also reads only the repo's own source, not what an installer downloads later. That's why the sandbox is the real protection and the scan is the early warning.

It also has to stay quiet on honest code. I ran it over the 150 most-starred Python, JavaScript and TypeScript repos on GitHub. It flagged one: lodash, for a vendored debugging script from 2009 that really does call eval(unescape(...)). A later run over 22 more repos produced two false alarms, on a large bundled Vue file and a chiptune synthesizer, and I tightened the rules that caused them.

What I'd take from this even if you never use Legwork

  • Stars are not a trust signal. Especially on a repo that's a few days old.
  • "Just try --help" is not safe. Code can run at import, before any flag is read.
  • AI agents make this worse. An assistant that can run shell commands will happily clone and run a trending repo because its README says it does what you asked for. Whatever it runs has your SSH keys, your files and your environment variables.
  • If an agent installs code for you, put a sandbox between that code and your home folder. Any sandbox.

Legwork is open source (MIT) and runs on macOS and Linux: https://github.com/kumarganduri/legwork

The full write-ups, including what failed along the way: the first finding and the top-ten trial. The repo also keeps a defanged copy of the first payload as a test fixture, with every encoded byte replaced by random data.

title: Scanning 3.8B Lines of Code Across 7,135 GitHub Repos: Measuring Cognitive Ownership & PR Review Risk
summary:
AI-assisted code generation is not inherently a software defect. Most high-performing engineering teams use coding assistants every day for boilerplate, migrations, and test scaffolding.

For CTOs, CISOs, and Staff Reviewers, the real systems problem is review velocity versus generation throughput: when diff volume scales faster than human review bandwidth, teams risk losing cognitive ownership, missing unverified third-party dependencies, and merging over-engineered abstractions.

To move this conversation away from guesswork and noisy probabilistic "AI detectors," we have been tracking deterministic static-analysis heuristics across 7,135 open-source GitHub repositories (~3.8 billion lines of code and 16.0 million pattern hits) on SlopCodeMonitor.

4 Governance Vectors Across 7,133 Repositories

Rather than guessing who or what wrote a function, the benchmark maps static findings into four operational review indices (0–100):

  • PR Review Velocity Impact (Mean: 22.28 / 100): Structural complexity, oversized functions, and branching density that slow down human pull-request triage.
  • Cognitive Ownership Risk (Mean: 13.93 / 100): Silent broad exception handling, opaque control-flow nesting, and patterns that obscure runtime failure modes.
  • Agent Over-Engineering Ratio (Mean: 12.5 / 100): Unnecessary wrapper layers, boilerplate proliferation, and premature abstraction.
  • Hallucinated Dependency & Supply-Chain Risk (Mean: 4.73 / 100): Unverified package surfaces and dependency hygiene signals relevant to AppSec and slopsquatting defense.

Important caveat: these scores are heuristic engineering prompts for human review, not proof of AI authorship or confirmed security vulnerabilities.

Language-Level Benchmarks

Structural review signals vary significantly across ecosystems depending on type systems, standard library breadth, and packaging conventions. You can explore the per-language distributions directly:

title: Rust 1.100 Is Out. I Installed It This Morning and Tried the Three Things That Actually Matter
summary:
Rust 1.100.0 landed on Thursday, November 12. Three days later I upgraded my own machine from 1.99.1 and spent the morning putting the headline features through their paces: the never type, custom allocators, and Cargo's two new supply-chain features. Everything below ran on my machine, and the numbers are the ones I actually saw.

The upgrade itself

One command, about ninety seconds, and rustc --version went from 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13) to 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09). Nothing broke on the way up. That matters, because this release does carry one change the release notes flag as potentially breaking, and I'll get to it.

The never type, ten years later

The headline is !, the never type. It's the type of an expression that never produces a value. A panic!(), an endless loop, a function that exits the process. People have been able to use it for years. But naming it anywhere a type goes, writing Result for a result that can never fail, took ten years and five failed stabilization attempts to land.

The first thing I tried was the obvious one:

let ok: Result<u32, !> = Ok(42);

It compiles, and it reads the way you'd hope. This result has no error case, and the type system now says so out loud. Infallible is now just an alias for !, which tidies up a decade of Result signatures.

The part worth paying attention to is the fallback change, because it's the one that can bite existing code. When the compiler can't work out what type a ! expression should be, it used to fall back to (). On 1.100 it falls back to ! instead, on every edition, not just 2024. I checked this directly with a snippet where the type is genuinely unconstrained: a closure that never runs, collecting into a Vec of unknown element type:

let v: Vec<_> = (0..0).map(|_| panic!()).collect();
println!("element type: {}", std::any::type_name_of_val(&v));

On 1.99.1 that prints alloc::vec::Vec<()>. On 1.100.0 it prints alloc::vec::Vec. Same code, different inferred type. Most code will never notice. The fallback only matters where a type was left completely unspecified. But if your build breaks after this upgrade and the error mentions ! where you expected (), this is the change to look at. The other two things the release notes flag for the same reason: closures now capture variables used in if let more precisely, and some Box implementations were generalised to arbitrary allocators, which can surface as new inference errors.

Custom allocators: Vec in my own arena

The second big item is the core of the allocator API, first proposed years ago and unstable until now. Vec and Box can live in an allocator you define, instead of the global one. I wrote a tiny bump allocator: a fixed 64 KiB buffer, a cursor, nothing else. Then I put a Vec inside it:

let bump = Bump::new();
let mut v: Vec<u32, &Bump> = Vec::new_in(&bump);
for i in 0..1000 {
    v.push(i * i);
}

It ran first try. The output:

Vec in bump arena: len=1000, sum=332833500, arena used=8176 bytes
Box in bump arena: 0xdeadbeef, arena used=8184 bytes

A thousand squares, 8,176 bytes of arena used. The Vec's four allocations (it grows 4, 8, 16… up to 4,096 bytes, plus alignment padding) land exactly where you'd expect, and a Box::new_in next to it takes 8 more bytes. The sum checks out against the closed form (999 × 1000 × 1999 / 6 = 332,833,500), so the Vec really holds what I think it holds.

Who is this for? Not most of us, honestly. If you're writing a game engine, an embedded runtime, or anything where allocation patterns are part of the design, this is the release you've been waiting for. Vec::new_in, Vec::with_capacity_in and Box::new_in are the whole story. If you're writing a web service, you'll probably never touch it, and that's fine. It's a foundation, not a feature you have to use.

Two smaller additions from the same release that I will use: bool::toggle() (finally, no more flag = !flag) and core::mem::DropGuard, which runs a closure when it drops while keeping the value usable in the meantime. Both worked exactly as documented.

Cargo's two supply-chain features

Cargo gets the most practical upgrade in this release, and both parts are about the same worry: the dependencies you pull in.

Unused dependency warnings. Cargo now tells you when a dependency in your manifest is never used, through the new cargo::unused_dependencies lint. I added itoa to a test project and used nothing from it:

warning: unused dependency `itoa`
  --> Cargo.toml:10:1
   |
10 | itoa = "1"
   | ^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `itoa`

Warn by default, and it becomes a hard error if you set it to deny in [lints.cargo]. I tried both, and the deny version fails the build with the same message as an error. This is the kind of lint that pays for itself the first time it catches a dependency someone added "just in case" three years ago.

Dependency cooldowns. Set registry.global-min-publish-age and the resolver skips crate versions published more recently than that age, unless they're already in your lockfile. The idea is simple. Most malicious crate versions get caught within days of publication, so waiting a week before adopting anything new closes that window. One gotcha I hit while setting it up: "7d" is rejected. The value has to read like "7 days":

error: invalid value for `registry.global-min-publish-age`:
expected a value of the form "N seconds/minutes/hours/days/weeks/months",
got: "7d"

With "7 days" in place, the build passed with the locked versions untouched. I should be honest about the limit of what I tested here: the protection only bites on a fresh resolve, when the resolver is choosing versions. My test project already had a lockfile, so I watched the config get accepted, not the resolver refuse a version. The next fresh project I start will be the real test.

Did anything get faster?

I timed clean release builds of a small project (serde, serde_json, clap) on both toolchains, twice each:

Toolchain Run 1 Run 2
1.99.1 29.1s 29.4s
1.100.0 31.1s 29.9s

No measurable difference. The 1.100 numbers sit inside the same noise band as 1.99.1, and a two-second spread on a 30-second build of a small project is not a finding. It's the machine breathing. Nobody should upgrade for compile speed. (The release does stabilise -Cprofile-sample-use, sample-based PGO, which is a real performance lever for production binaries. But that's a profiling setup, not something a clean-build timer would show.)

Should you upgrade?

Yes, and the checklist is short. Run your test suite on 1.100 before you commit to it. The fallback change is narrow but real, and it's exactly the kind of thing that shows up in one weird corner of a big codebase rather than everywhere at once. If you maintain a library, the Box generalisation is the other one to watch for. Everything else in this release is additive: the never type, the allocator API, the Cargo lints and the cooldowns are all things you can adopt when they fit, not things you have to deal with on upgrade day.

The round number is a coincidence, mostly. Rust 1.100 is not a new era and not a rewrite. It's a solid release with one ten-year-old feature finally landing, one genuinely useful Cargo upgrade, and a small breaking change hiding in the compatibility notes. Read those notes, run your tests, then upgrade. That's the whole plan.

Sources

  • Rust 1.100.0 release notes: dev-doc.rust-lang.org/stable/releases.html (Version 1.100.0, 2026-11-12)
  • Never type, custom allocators, Cargo lints and cooldowns, compatibility notes: same page, sections Language / Libraries / Stabilized APIs / Cargo / Compatibility Notes
  • Every number in this article comes from runs on my own machine on 2026-11-15: rustc 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09), upgraded from rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13)

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

When the compiler can't work out what type a ! expression should be, it used to fall back to (). On 1.100 it falls back to ! instead, on every edition, not just 2024. I checked this directly with a snippet where the type is genuinely unconstrained: a closure that never runs, collecting into a Vec of unknown element type:

let v: Vec<_> = (0..0).map(|_| panic!()).collect();
println!("element type: {}", std::any::type_name_of_val(&v));

On 1.99.1 that prints alloc::vec::Vec<()>. On 1.100.0 it prints alloc::vec::Vec. Same code, different inferred type. Most code will never notice. The fallback only matters where a type was left completely unspecified. But if your build breaks after this upgrade and the error mentions ! where you expected (), this is the change to look at. The other two things the release notes flag for the same reason: closures now capture variables used in if let more precisely, and some Box implementations were generalised to arbitrary allocators, which can surface as new inference errors.

Custom allocators: Vec in my own arena

The second big item is the core of the allocator API, first proposed years ago and unstable until now. Vec and Box can live in an allocator you define, instead of the global one. I wrote a tiny bump allocator: a fixed 64 KiB buffer, a cursor, nothing else. Then I put a Vec inside it:

let bump = Bump::new();
let mut v: Vec<u32, &Bump> = Vec::new_in(&bump);
for i in 0..1000 {
    v.push(i * i);
}

It ran first try. The output:

Vec in bump arena: len=1000, sum=332833500, arena used=8176 bytes
Box in bump arena: 0xdeadbeef, arena used=8184 bytes

A thousand squares, 8,176 bytes of arena used. The Vec's four allocations (it grows 4, 8, 16… up to 4,096 bytes, plus alignment padding) land exactly where you'd expect, and a Box::new_in next to it takes 8 more bytes. The sum checks out against the closed form (999 × 1000 × 1999 / 6 = 332,833,500), so the Vec really holds what I think it holds.

Who is this for? Not most of us, honestly. If you're writing a game engine, an embedded runtime, or anything where allocation patterns are part of the design, this is the release you've been waiting for. Vec::new_in, Vec::with_capacity_in and Box::new_in are the whole story. If you're writing a web service, you'll probably never touch it, and that's fine. It's a foundation, not a feature you have to use.

Two smaller additions from the same release that I will use: bool::toggle() (finally, no more flag = !flag) and core::mem::DropGuard, which runs a closure when it drops while keeping the value usable in the meantime. Both worked exactly as documented.

Cargo's two supply-chain features

Cargo gets the most practical upgrade in this release, and both parts are about the same worry: the dependencies you pull in.

Unused dependency warnings. Cargo now tells you when a dependency in your manifest is never used, through the new cargo::unused_dependencies lint. I added itoa to a test project and used nothing from it:

warning: unused dependency `itoa`
  --> Cargo.toml:10:1
   |
10 | itoa = "1"
   | ^^^^^^^^^^
   |
   = note: `cargo::unused_dependencies` is set to `warn` by default
help: consider removing the dependency on `itoa`

Warn by default, and it becomes a hard error if you set it to deny in [lints.cargo]. I tried both, and the deny version fails the build with the same message as an error. This is the kind of lint that pays for itself the first time it catches a dependency someone added "just in case" three years ago.

Dependency cooldowns. Set registry.global-min-publish-age and the resolver skips crate versions published more recently than that age, unless they're already in your lockfile. The idea is simple. Most malicious crate versions get caught within days of publication, so waiting a week before adopting anything new closes that window. One gotcha I hit while setting it up: "7d" is rejected. The value has to read like "7 days":

error: invalid value for `registry.global-min-publish-age`:
expected a value of the form "N seconds/minutes/hours/days/weeks/months",
got: "7d"

With "7 days" in place, the build passed with the locked versions untouched. I should be honest about the limit of what I tested here: the protection only bites on a fresh resolve, when the resolver is choosing versions. My test project already had a lockfile, so I watched the config get accepted, not the resolver refuse a version. The next fresh project I start will be the real test.

Did anything get faster?

I timed clean release builds of a small project (serde, serde_json, clap) on both toolchains, twice each:

Toolchain Run 1 Run 2
1.99.1 29.1s 29.4s
1.100.0 31.1s 29.9s

No measurable difference. The 1.100 numbers sit inside the same noise band as 1.99.1, and a two-second spread on a 30-second build of a small project is not a finding. It's the machine breathing. Nobody should upgrade for compile speed. (The release does stabilise -Cprofile-sample-use, sample-based PGO, which is a real performance lever for production binaries. But that's a profiling setup, not something a clean-build timer would show.)

Should you upgrade?

Yes, and the checklist is short. Run your test suite on 1.100 before you commit to it. The fallback change is narrow but real, and it's exactly the kind of thing that shows up in one weird corner of a big codebase rather than everywhere at once. If you maintain a library, the Box generalisation is the other one to watch for. Everything else in this release is additive: the never type, the allocator API, the Cargo lints and the cooldowns are all things you can adopt when they fit, not things you have to deal with on upgrade day.

The round number is a coincidence, mostly. Rust 1.100 is not a new era and not a rewrite. It's a solid release with one ten-year-old feature finally landing, one genuinely useful Cargo upgrade, and a small breaking change hiding in the compatibility notes. Read those notes, run your tests, then upgrade. That's the whole plan.

  • Never type, custom allocators, Cargo lints and cooldowns, compatibility notes: same page, sections Language / Libraries / Stabilized APIs / Cargo / Compatibility Notes
  • Every number in this article comes from runs on my own machine on 2026-11-15: rustc 1.100.0 (0ef1bc386 2026-11-09), upgraded from rustc 1.99.1 (58cf8f9c3 2026-10-13)

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

title: A full web controller for vMix: control everything from your browser
summary:
vMix runs on one computer, usually in the studio, and the person who needs to control it is not always standing next to it. A colleague wants to see what is on air. An operator has a problem with the audio. You want to know how long the current video has left.

vMix has a built-in Web Controller for this, and we tried it first. It is minimal: it shows each input as a type letter and a number, such as V 5, so during a live show you have to remember what V 5 is, and it is meant for a few inputs and simple switching. We wanted the whole vMix on a web page, so we built vMix Master.

What is on the page

vMix Master is laid out like vMix itself, so it feels familiar from the first minute.

  • Program and preview with large timers, a position slider, Restart and Play/Pause, and six transition buttons: Quick Play, Cut, Stinger 1, Stinger 2, Fade and FTB.
  • Every input by name, with its number, its audio level, and what is on air and in preview. 05 Opening Video.mp4 instead of V 5.
  • A tile for each input with overlays 1 to 6, loop, volume, and send-to-bus buttons.
  • Audio buses with live level meters.
  • Function buttons for most of the vMix API, grouped by what they do: outputs (external, SRT, recording, streaming), transitions, audio, overlays, playback, countdowns, titles, layers and picture, PTZ, playlists and scripts. A raw request box takes any other function.
  • Works on a phone or tablet, and can be installed as an app from Chrome.

It needs nothing installed. It is a static page that talks straight to the Web Controller your vMix already has, from your browser, over your local network. You can try everything without vMix in the live demo, which runs simulated systems inside the page.

How we use it day to day

During a session our operators sit in the studio and the support team does not. From the same page on the local network we can open any of their systems and help without going to the room:

  • If the audio is too loud, lower the volume or the gain.
  • To see how long a video has left, and so how long until they go live, open that system and read the timer.
  • To start or stop a stream, press the function button instead of asking someone to find it.

A bonus: several vMix systems as one

Our setup is unusual, and this part grew out of it. We stream live sessions in English, translated into German, French, Russian, Arabic and more, and each language runs on its own vMix system with its own copy of the media. When English plays a video, every other language has to play the same video in its translated version at the same moment.

So vMix Master can group systems. Add the English, German, French and Arabic systems, put them in one group, and mark English as the master. Whatever you do on the master, such as a transition or an audio change, is sent to every system in the group at once.

We used the same idea at events with vertical and horizontal screens in the hall. One vMix played the vertical version of every video and another played the horizontal one, and one click switched both.

Group Compare checks that the systems in a group are set up alike. It matches inputs by the number at the start of their name. A different number or order on one system is an error. A video on one system and a slide on another, for the same number, is a warning about the type. The same video more than 5 seconds longer or shorter on one system is a warning too, and it also checks audio buses, call sources and overlay layers. It is how we find a missing file or a wrong translation when we prepare new content, before the session instead of during it.

For the translations themselves we later moved to a small script that runs inside vMix on each translation system and follows the English one, so those operators never need the website. The slave scripts are free and live in the same repository. vMix Master is still what we use to monitor and compare the systems, and to step in when something goes wrong.

Other options

Bitfocus Companion is a good choice if you want Stream Deck style buttons and hardware surfaces. It is a separate app, and you build your own pages. OBS users have web control panels such as obs-web, and we could not find an equivalent for vMix with this much of the interface, which is why we made one.

What it doesn't do

  • It cannot use a Web Controller that has a password. vMix asks for the password in a header that a browser may only send after vMix agrees to it, and vMix does not agree, so Chrome blocks the request and the box shows Web Controller needs a password (401). Leave the password off and keep the port on a trusted local network. On the vMix computer itself you can instead tick Allow software on this computer access without login in the Web Controller settings and use 127.0.0.1 as the address.
  • It has no hardware control surface support.
  • It is made for Chrome, which asks once whether the page may reach devices on your local network.
  • The slave scripts need vMix 4K or Pro, the editions that have scripting.

Try it

vMix Master is free and open source (MIT). Open the demo to look around. To use it with your own vMix, enable the Web Controller in vMix (default port 8088) and open the hosted app. The documentation explains how to connect your systems.

If something you need from a vMix control panel is missing, open an issue and tell us. And if it helps you, a star on the repository helps other vMix operators find it.

title: Fixing a Concurrency Bug an Architect Caught in My Flink-Qdrant Connector
summary:
The connector nobody had built yet

Apache Flink didn't have an official SQL connector for Qdrant, the vector database. I use both — Flink for streaming pipelines, Qdrant for the embedding store downstream — so I built flink-connector-qdrant to close that gap: a Flink SQL sink that upserts points into Qdrant directly from a streaming job, no glue code in between.

It shipped, people started using it, and then an architect reviewing it on LinkedIn pointed out something I'd missed.

The bug

My upsert path stored a version number per point so that if the same ID arrived twice, the connector could tell which write was newer and keep that one. Straightforward, except for one thing: storing a version number alone doesn't guarantee atomic ordering under concurrent writers.

Picture two parallel sink tasks racing on the same point ID. Writer A has version 5, writer B has version 6. There's no guarantee B's write lands after A's just because its version number is higher — depending on timing, A can still land last and silently overwrite the newer data. A bare version field tells you which value should win; it doesn't make the database enforce that when two writes are in flight at the same time.

That's a real data-correctness bug, not a style nit. In a streaming sink, "newer data wins" is the whole point of upserts.

The fix

I added an opt-in version-field option: when configured, the connector deduplicates by highest version within a batch before the Qdrant write goes out, instead of trusting Qdrant to sort it out writer by writer. Same version field the architect was looking at, but the ordering guarantee now lives on my side of the wire, where I actually control it.

I shipped it as three separate commits — a fix for the dedup logic, a feat for the opt-in config surface, and a docs commit explaining when to turn it on — instead of squashing it into one. Reviewing a bug fix is easier when you're not also reviewing a new feature flag in the same diff, and it meant the person who raised the issue could actually see the fix land commit by commit rather than taking my word for it.

The other repo

Same week, I pushed multi-cluster support into apache-flink-mcp-server — it lets AI assistants talk to a Flink cluster over MCP (Model Context Protocol), but until now it only knew about one cluster at a time, which doesn't match how anyone actually runs Flink. It also picked up its listing on the Glama MCP directory.

Neither of these projects is glamorous. They're the kind of infrastructure that's only interesting when it's wrong. But getting real review from someone who actually reads the code, and being able to turn that into a fix the same week, is the part of open source that's worth writing about.

If you're running vector search behind a Flink pipeline, or you want an AI assistant that can actually see what's happening in your Flink cluster, both repos are open for issues and PRs.

title: Amazon Vendor Central Self-Service EDI SFTP: Handling 850/855/856/810 Turnarounds, REF*BX ARN & 820 Multi-ADX Deductions in TypeScript
summary:
If you supply Amazon as a 1P vendor on Vendor Central, you eventually hit the limits of the web portal: manually typing shipment quantities, accidentally locking an 856 ASN before Amazon finishes reallocating the destination Fulfillment Center (N1*ST), or spending hours reconciling multi-page 820 remittance PDFs against shortage and co-op chargebacks.

Amazon Vendor Central includes a free Self-Service EDI SFTP channel (850 in → 855 / 856 / 810 out, plus 820 remittance advices) that requires zero third-party VAN fees. Yet small suppliers and integration engineers routinely get tripped up by four X12 004010 / 005010 subtleties that trigger automatic $250–$1,500+ chargebacks.

This engineering guide breaks down the exact segment structures, TypeScript parsing patterns, and pre-flight validation checks needed to run a clean Amazon 1P EDI turnaround workflow.

1. The Amazon 1P EDI Turnaround Loop (Why Portal ASN Locks Hurt)

In Vendor Central, Amazon frequently reassigns destination FCs (N1*ST 4-letter SAN codes) or issues an 860 PO Change hours after releasing an 850 Purchase Order. If you generate and submit an 856 ASN immediately on receipt, that BSN02 Shipment ID and its MAN*GM SSCC-18 carton barcodes lock to the stale FC.

With Self-Service SFTP, decouple acknowledgment from dispatch:

  1. Ingest 850 PO → validate BEG03 (PO#), PO1 item identifiers (BP / UP / IN), PO4 case-pack multiples, and N1*ST ship-to FC code.
  2. Send 855 PO Acknowledgment immediately with line-level status (ACK*IA accepted, ACK*IQ partial qty, ACK*IB backorder, ACK*IR rejected).
  3. Hold 856 ASN & 4x6" GS1-128 printing until Routing Confirmation returns your ARN (Amazon Reference Number).
  4. Emit 856 (REF*BX*) + 810 Invoice (BIG04*) mirrored to the exact X12 version (004010 / 005010) and ISA15 (T test vs. P production) flag from the inbound 850.

2. Threading REF*BX (ARN) & SSCC-18 Uniqueness Across 856 & 4x6" Labels

Amazon's receiving dock requires two non-negotiable links between your physical cartons, your 856 ASN, and your routing request:

  • Amazon Reference Number (REF*BX): Passed at the Shipment (HL*S) level on the 856 ASN (REF*BX*ARN123456789~) and mirrored onto the human-readable zone of your 4x6" GS1-128 shipping label.
  • Non-Colliding SSCC-18 (MAN*GM): Every physical carton (HL*P) needs a globally unique 20-digit 00 + SSCC-18 barcode with a valid GS1 Modulo-10 check digit. Reusing a serial number from a voided ASN—or having two warehouse packing stations emit the same serial simultaneously—causes an immediate receiving scan collision. 
// Checking for duplicate SSCC-18 barcodes inside a single outbound 856 ASN
export function findDuplicateSscc18InAsn(segments: string[][]): string[] {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  const duplicates = new Set<string>();

  for (const seg of segments) {
    if (seg[0] === 'MAN' && seg[1] === 'GM' && seg[2]) {
      const code = seg[2].trim();
      if (seen.has(code)) duplicates.add(code);
      seen.add(code);
    }
  }
  return [...duplicates];
}

Demo-Prefix Guard: Never let a GS1 documentation example prefix like 0614141 leak into a production ISA15=P shipment or 4x6" PDF label—retailers treat it as an unmapped vendor barcode and fine per carton.

3. Parsing 820 Remittances Without Dropping Multiple ADX Deductions

A subtle bug in naive EDI 820 parsers happens inside the ENT -> RMR -> ADX remittance loop. One paid invoice (RMR*IV*INV-10482**2500.00*2500.00~) often carries multiple consecutive ADX adjustment segments—for example, a co-op marketing allowance, a shortage claim, and a late-ASN fine—plus standalone ADX segments outside an RMR loop.

If your parser assigns currentInvoice.adjustment = parseAdx(seg) instead of pushing into an array, every subsequent ADX silently overwrites the previous deduction!

export interface RemittanceAdjustment {
  amount: number;
  reasonCode: string;
  referenceId?: string;
}

export interface RemittanceInvoiceLine {
  invoiceNumber: string;
  netPaid: number;
  grossBilled: number;
  adjustments: RemittanceAdjustment[];
  unexplainedVariance: number;
}

export function accumulateRmrAndAdx(segments: string[][]): {
  lines: RemittanceInvoiceLine[];
  standaloneAdjustments: RemittanceAdjustment[];
} {
  const lines: RemittanceInvoiceLine[] = [];
  const standaloneAdjustments: RemittanceAdjustment[] = [];
  let current: RemittanceInvoiceLine | null = null;

  for (const seg of segments) {
    if (seg[0] === 'RMR') {
      current = {
        invoiceNumber: seg[2] || '',
        netPaid: Number(seg[4] || 0),
        grossBilled: Number(seg[5] || 0),
        adjustments: [],
        unexplainedVariance: 0,
      };
      lines.push(current);
    } else if (seg[0] === 'ADX') {
      const adj: RemittanceAdjustment = {
        amount: Number(seg[1] || 0),
        reasonCode: seg[2] || '',
        referenceId: seg[4] || undefined,
      };
      if (current) {
        current.adjustments.push(adj);
      } else {
        standaloneAdjustments.push(adj);
      }
    } else if (seg[0] === 'ENT' || seg[0] === 'SE') {
      current = null;
    }
  }

  for (const line of lines) {
    const adxSum = line.adjustments.reduce((acc, item) => acc + item.amount, 0);
    line.unexplainedVariance = Number(
      (line.grossBilled + adxSum - line.netPaid).toFixed(2)
    );
  }

  return { lines, standaloneAdjustments };
}

Checking unexplainedVariance to the penny immediately flags discrepancies before your 30-day Vendor Central dispute window expires.

4. Testing Without Uploading Wholesale Pricing

If you want to inspect real Amazon 850 / 824 payloads or validate your turnaround files before dropping them onto Amazon's SFTP outbox:

  • Open-Source Sample Payloads (MIT): laozhang713/ansi-x12-edi-sample-files on GitHub includes sanitized Amazon 850 and 824 application advice test fixtures.
  • Browser-Local Linter & Turnaround Workbench: I built EDIParse's Amazon Vendor Central EDI 850/856/810 Converter and EDI 820 Remittance Parser to parse X12 files 100% in volatile browser RAM (zero raw order storage on our servers, no AS2/VAN transport hosted) and output SFTP-ready 855 + 856 (REF*BX ARN) + 810 + 4x6" GS1-128 PDFs.

Amazon Vendor Central includes a free Self-Service EDI SFTP channel (850 in → 855 / 856 / 810 out, plus 820 remittance advices) that requires zero third-party VAN fees. Yet small suppliers and integration engineers routinely get tripped up by four X12 004010 / 005010 subtleties that trigger automatic $250–$1,500+ chargebacks.

This engineering guide breaks down the exact segment structures, TypeScript parsing patterns, and pre-flight validation checks needed to run a clean Amazon 1P EDI turnaround workflow.

1. The Amazon 1P EDI Turnaround Loop (Why Portal ASN Locks Hurt)

In Vendor Central, Amazon frequently reassigns destination FCs (N1*ST 4-letter SAN codes) or issues an 860 PO Change hours after releasing an 850 Purchase Order. If you generate and submit an 856 ASN immediately on receipt, that BSN02 Shipment ID and its MAN*GM SSCC-18 carton barcodes lock to the stale FC.

With Self-Service SFTP, decouple acknowledgment from dispatch:

  1. Ingest 850 PO → validate BEG03 (PO#), PO1 item identifiers (BP / UP / IN), PO4 case-pack multiples, and N1*ST ship-to FC code.
  2. Send 855 PO Acknowledgment immediately with line-level status (ACK*IA accepted, ACK*IQ partial qty, ACK*IB backorder, ACK*IR rejected).
  3. Hold 856 ASN & 4x6" GS1-128 printing until Routing Confirmation returns your ARN (Amazon Reference Number).
  4. Emit 856 (REF*BX*) + 810 Invoice (BIG04*) mirrored to the exact X12 version (004010 / 005010) and ISA15 (T test vs. P production) flag from the inbound 850.

2. Threading REF*BX (ARN) & SSCC-18 Uniqueness Across 856 & 4x6" Labels

Amazon's receiving dock requires two non-negotiable links between your physical cartons, your 856 ASN, and your routing request:

  • Amazon Reference Number (REF*BX): Passed at the Shipment (HL*S) level on the 856 ASN (REF*BX*ARN123456789~) and mirrored onto the human-readable zone of your 4x6" GS1-128 shipping label.
  • Non-Colliding SSCC-18 (MAN*GM): Every physical carton (HL*P) needs a globally unique 20-digit 00 + SSCC-18 barcode with a valid GS1 Modulo-10 check digit. Reusing a serial number from a voided ASN—or having two warehouse packing stations emit the same serial simultaneously—causes an immediate receiving scan collision. 
// Checking for duplicate SSCC-18 barcodes inside a single outbound 856 ASN
export function findDuplicateSscc18InAsn(segments: string[][]): string[] {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  const duplicates = new Set<string>();

  for (const seg of segments) {
    if (seg[0] === 'MAN' && seg[1] === 'GM' && seg[2]) {
      const code = seg[2].trim();
      if (seen.has(code)) duplicates.add(code);
      seen.add(code);
    }
  }
  return [...duplicates];
}

Demo-Prefix Guard: Never let a GS1 documentation example prefix like 0614141 leak into a production ISA15=P shipment or 4x6" PDF label—retailers treat it as an unmapped vendor barcode and fine per carton.

3. Parsing 820 Remittances Without Dropping Multiple ADX Deductions

A subtle bug in naive EDI 820 parsers happens inside the ENT -> RMR -> ADX remittance loop. One paid invoice (RMR*IV*INV-10482**2500.00*2500.00~) often carries multiple consecutive ADX adjustment segments—for example, a co-op marketing allowance, a shortage claim, and a late-ASN fine—plus standalone ADX segments outside an RMR loop.

If your parser assigns currentInvoice.adjustment = parseAdx(seg) instead of pushing into an array, every subsequent ADX silently overwrites the previous deduction!

export interface RemittanceAdjustment {
  amount: number;
  reasonCode: string;
  referenceId?: string;
}

export interface RemittanceInvoiceLine {
  invoiceNumber: string;
  netPaid: number;
  grossBilled: number;
  adjustments: RemittanceAdjustment[];
  unexplainedVariance: number;
}

export function accumulateRmrAndAdx(segments: string[][]): {
  lines: RemittanceInvoiceLine[];
  standaloneAdjustments: RemittanceAdjustment[];
} {
  const lines: RemittanceInvoiceLine[] = [];
  const standaloneAdjustments: RemittanceAdjustment[] = [];
  let current: RemittanceInvoiceLine | null = null;

  for (const seg of segments) {
    if (seg[0] === 'RMR') {
      current = {
        invoiceNumber: seg[2] || '',
        netPaid: Number(seg[4] || 0),
        grossBilled: Number(seg[5] || 0),
        adjustments: [],
        unexplainedVariance: 0,
      };
      lines.push(current);
    } else if (seg[0] === 'ADX') {
      const adj: RemittanceAdjustment = {
        amount: Number(seg[1] || 0),
        reasonCode: seg[2] || '',
        referenceId: seg[4] || undefined,
      };
      if (current) {
        current.adjustments.push(adj);
      } else {
        standaloneAdjustments.push(adj);
      }
    } else if (seg[0] === 'ENT' || seg[0] === 'SE') {
      current = null;
    }
  }

  for (const line of lines) {
    const adxSum = line.adjustments.reduce((acc, item) => acc + item.amount, 0);
    line.unexplainedVariance = Number(
      (line.grossBilled + adxSum - line.netPaid).toFixed(2)
    );
  }

  return { lines, standaloneAdjustments };
}

Checking unexplainedVariance to the penny immediately flags discrepancies before your 30-day Vendor Central dispute window expires.

4. Testing Without Uploading Wholesale Pricing

If you want to inspect real Amazon 850 / 824 payloads or validate your turnaround files before dropping them onto Amazon's SFTP outbox:

title: I got tired of Redis and Kafka eating my RAM, so I rebuilt them in Rust hitting 1.6M RPS (as a student)
summary:
Hey everyone, I’m Yasir. I’m an 18-year-old software engineering student from Pakistan, and for the last few months, I’ve been going down a very deep, very complex rabbit hole: Systems Programming in Rust.
When I started learning about distributed systems, I noticed a recurring theme: tools like Apache Kafka and Redis are absolute industry standards, but they come with a catch. Kafka relies heavily on the JVM (hello, GC pauses and massive memory footprints), and standard in-memory stores often hit bottlenecks when scaling across modern multi-core CPUs due to OS-level thread contention and locks.
I didn't have the budget to run massive AWS clusters for my personal projects. I needed something that could run on a potato but still handle enterprise-level throughput.
So, I decided to build my own.
Enter Velocity-Suite (Velocity-MQ & VelocityDB)
I built two core **infrastructure pieces entirely from scratch in Rust:
Velocity-MQ: A zero-GC, lock-free message queue (Kafka alternative).
**VelocityDB: A thread-per-core, lock-free in-memory store (Redis alternative).
My goal wasn't just to write another wrapper. I wanted to bypass traditional OS bottlenecks entirely. Here is the architecture that made it happen:
1_. Bypassing the Kernel with io_uring
Traditional synchronous I/O or even epoll wasn't cutting it for the persistent disk I/O I wanted. I integrated Linux io_uring for asynchronous I/O. By using O_DIRECT, the system completely bypasses the OS page cache. This means zero-copy transfers straight from the disk to the application memory, resulting in microsecond latencies._
2. Thread-per-Core Architecture
Instead of having multiple threads fighting over a shared state (and melting the CPU with context switches), I used a thread-per-core model. Each thread owns its data. No locks, no mutexes blocking the hot path.
3. Lock-Free Concurrency
To allow threads to communicate without slowing down, I heavily utilized lock-free data structures (like ring buffers) and atomic pointers. Fighting the Rust borrow checker while dealing with std::sync::atomic memory ordering (Acquire/Release semantics) was probably the hardest thing I’ve ever done, but the performance payoff was insane.
The Benchmarks 🚀
After weeks of debugging segmentation faults and memory ordering bugs, I finally ran the benchmarks on my local machine:
VelocityDB: **Reached **1.6M+ Requests Per Second (RPS). Click this : https://github.com/developer-yasir/velocitydb .
Velocity-MQ: Pushed 600k+ ops/sec with virtually zero garbage collection overhead. https://github.com/developer-yasir/Velocity-MQ
Running this on minimal RAM felt like a superpower.
Why I am sharing this (I need your help!)
I am incredibly proud of what I've built, but I am also just a 1st-semester CS student. I know for a fact that my code isn't perfect. Systems programming is brutal, and edge cases around memory barriers and crash recovery are terrifying.
I am putting this out here because I want to learn from the best.
If you are a senior Rustacean, a systems engineer, or just someone who loves high-performance backends, I would be honored if you could look at my code.
Roast my architecture.
Tell me where my memory ordering is flawed.
Open an issue if you see a bug.
You can check out the code here:
🔗 https://github.com/developer-yasir/

If you find this project interesting or helpful, dropping a ⭐ on the repo would mean the world to me and keep me motivated to keep building!
Let me know your thoughts in the comments. Let's talk about io_uring and Rust!

title: Why "it works on my machine" isn't enough for open-source QA
summary:
When you build an open-source testing framework, you reach a point where the code is done, the tests are passing, and the features are implemented.

For a lot of developers, that's the end of the line. "It works on my machine. I'm done."

But for a framework to be truly valuable to a client, that is only the halfway point. The code existing is not the same thing as the code being reliable.

I've been building Praman, an open-source QA engine in Python. The test suite just crossed 910 passing tests. The API automation, browser sessions, configuration, and reporting are all implemented. But as I look at my roadmap, I realize the hardest work is still ahead: proving it actually works in the real world.

Here is why building a framework for real clients requires a different mindset.

When you build a feature, it's easy to mark it as "done" in your head. But a QA framework requires independent validation.

If I build a wheel and test it locally, that proves the wheel builds. It doesn't prove that a developer in a different environment can install it, import it, and run a test without it breaking. To prove that, I have to build the wheel, spin up a completely isolated Python 3.12 environment, install the wheel from scratch, and run an external client smoke test.

Only then is the packaging "done."

Phase 5 of my roadmap is AI-assisted testing. It's the most exciting part. I want to build LLM integration, failure analysis, and suggested fixes.

But I am deliberately not starting it yet.

If I introduce an AI agent that analyzes failures, but my JSON failure reports are inconsistent, the AI will give me bad analysis. If I add LLM code generation, but my isolated installation tests aren't passing, the AI will generate tests that don't run.

You cannot build advanced AI features on top of a shaky foundation. The execution, reporting, and evidence systems have to be bulletproof first.

I created a "Foundation Release Candidate" checklist for the next milestone. It doesn't just ask "does the code exist?" It asks:

  • Does the latest wheel build and install independently?
  • Do the external client tests pass?
  • Are failure screenshots and redaction verified?
  • Does the latest hosted GitHub Actions run succeed?

If any of these are false, the foundation isn't ready.

A passing test suite is a great milestone. It means you have 910 examples of your code doing the right thing. But a reliable framework is not just about the tests you write. It's about isolated client installation, clean CI pipelines, and documenting exactly what has been verified.

If you are building a tool for other developers, don't just ask if it works on your machine. Ask if it works on theirs.

You can see the current progress and the roadmap on the repository: https://github.com/pranromumu/praman

title: I tested whether a 4B model could replace a 12B one in a tool-using agent. My first test was wrong.
summary:
Two pre-registered runs on local models, a reader's correction between them, and the one place the small model still breaks.

I wanted to know whether a 4B local model could replace a 12B one in a small tool-using agent. I ran it as an experiment, with the prediction written down before each run. Both models ran on Ollama on one laptop, at temperature 0.7, with no API.

The set-up

  • 24 order-desk tasks: refund an order, refund and add a note, check stock and add a note.
  • Each task ran clean and under three injected tool faults: a timeout, a one-off error, an empty result. That makes 96 task-and-fault combinations per round.
  • Baseline: gemma4 12B. Candidate: qwen3.5 4B. Same prompt, same tools, same retry settings.
  • The rule for the verdict was fixed before the run: is the 4B within 10 points of the 12B?

Run 1: my prediction lost

I predicted the 4B would be close enough. It was not. The 12B passed 96 of 96. The 4B passed 70 of 96, and the run stopped after one round with a verdict of BLOCK.

Most of the failures were one behaviour. In 21 of the 26, the 4B was asked to check stock for an order and its only call was to the stock tool, with the order id as the product code. It never looked the order up.

A reader caught a flaw in the test

In my set-up that wrong call raised an exception and ended the trial. The model never saw "unknown SKU". So I had measured "makes a wrong first call, where a wrong call is fatal". I had not measured "cannot do the task". I published a correction and ran it again.

Run 2: the error goes back to the model

One change, the same for both models: a tool's error is returned to the model as a message. My prediction, written first: inconclusive.

  • 12B: 480 of 480.
  • 4B: 428 of 480 (89%).
  • The 4B made the wrong first call about as often as before: in 21 of 32 stock-note trials in run 1, and in 108 of 160 in run 2.
  • Shown the error, it looked the order up next in 106 of those 108, and 68 of the 108 passed.
  • Only 2 of 480 trials never did the lookup at all.

The test could not decide whether the 4B is within 10 points of the 12B. The gap landed at 10.8 points. So the verdict is INCONCLUSIVE: the run crossed neither the PASS nor the BLOCK threshold.

Where it still breaks

Two things going wrong in one trial. When the 4B made the wrong first call and then the lookup came back empty (the injected fault), it passed 0 of 26. In 21 of the 26 it read the error, looked the order up once, got nothing back, and stopped. The 12B retried the empty lookup every time, 120 of 120.

Where the wrong first call was the only lasting problem (no injected fault, or a timeout that a retry clears), the 4B went on to pass 52 of 58.

What I took from it

  • Know whether your tools raise their errors or return them. Here it changed what the test measured: in run 2, 77 of the 4B's 428 passes came after a tool error that would have ended the trial under run 1's set-up.
  • In this suite, looking at one problem at a time flattered the 4B. Half of its 52 failures in run 2 (26) were the compound case above.
  • I did not see any of this by reading sample outputs. I saw it by counting what each trial did with its tools.

Limits

One suite, one prompt, two models, one machine. The two runs used different seeds, so 73% against 89% is two observations, not a measured effect of returning errors. The breakdowns were chosen after seeing the data. None of this says anything about these models in general.

Check it yourself

The harness is my own open-source tool, ARCI. It runs a baseline and a candidate on the same tasks with injected tool faults and gives PASS, BLOCK or INCONCLUSIVE with a stated error bound.

  • Both runs, both pre-registrations and the correction
  • The raw records of every trial, with the command that re-derives both verdicts
  • The same comparison on your own two models
  • Repository

If you have measured this on other small models, I would like to know: does returning tool errors close most of the gap, or is that specific to this pair?

The numbers were recounted from the stored trial records before publishing, and those records are public at the links above. First published on my blog, Real or Noise.

title: Three more tools, three more countries: Bangladesh's new tax slabs, Sri Lanka's take-home pay and the hidden GPS in your photos
summary:
Some tools answer a question you ask once a year, when the tax return is due. Some answer a question you never thought to ask at all — like what your photo tells a stranger about where you were standing when you took it. This week I added three of both kinds to RozKaTool — free, no sign-up, everything runs in your browser — and each one reaches a different corner of Asia.

RozKaTool is now at 76 free tools, and the series keeps spreading: Nepal, Thailand, Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia so far.

1. Bangladesh: a third of your salary is exempt before the slabs even start

Bangladesh rewrote its personal income tax for income year 2025-26 under the Finance Act 2026, and the headline detail is one most people miss: a salaried employee is exempt on one-third of their salary, capped at ৳5,00,000 — before any slab is applied. The tax-free limit is ৳4,00,000 for a general taxpayer, ৳4,50,000 for women and senior citizens aged 65 or above, ৳5,25,000 for third-gender taxpayers and persons with disability, and ৳5,50,000 for gazetted freedom fighters.

Above the limit, the slabs run 10% on the next ৳3,00,000, 15% on the next ৳4,00,000, 20% on the next ৳5,00,000, 25% on the next ৳20,00,000 and 30% on the rest. An investment rebate — the lowest of 3% of taxable income, 15% of your allowable investment, or ৳10,00,000 — comes off the slab tax, and a flat ৳5,000 minimum tax applies once your income is above the tax-free limit, even if the slab tax is lower. Individual returns for this income year are due by 30 November 2026 (Tax Day).

Bangladesh Income Tax Calculator 2025-26 — enter your annual income, pick your category, and see the slab-by-slab tax, the rebate and the final amount. A general salaried taxpayer earning ৳12,00,000 a year gets a ৳4,00,000 salary exemption, leaving ৳8,00,000 taxable — tax of ৳45,000 for the year.

2. Sri Lanka: Rs. 150,000 a month is tax-free — and your EPF does not lower the tax

Sri Lanka's APIT (the PAYE tax your employer deducts every month) starts only after Rs. 150,000 a month — Rs. 1,800,000 a year — of personal relief. Above that, the rates for years of assessment 2025/26 and 2026/27 run 6% on the next Rs. 1,000,000, 18% on the next Rs. 500,000, 24% on the next Rs. 500,000, 30% on the next Rs. 500,000 and 36% above Rs. 4,300,000.

title: Which commit did those checks actually verify?
summary:
First published on openspec-ui.dev.

Imagine a pull request that targets a release branch. You ran the tests yesterday, committed a fix this morning, and still have one edit in your editor. To review the PR, you need a diff against the release branch and a way to tell which commit those tests covered.

In OpenSpec Workbench 0.108.0, open PR Review on the change's Pipeline card. It compares committed work with the merge base of the PR target and flags the local edits left outside that comparison. Workbench can use the default branch for a labelled preview while the PR target is unknown.

Recorded mechanical checks show whether their revision matches the head in the review. Earlier results are marked as historical, and records without a revision are marked as unknown. The verify agent's outcome has its own entry. Copy PR summary carries the comparison and those qualifications into the PR as Markdown.

This release also adds Send Feedback, which opens a GitHub issue draft, and a diagnostic preview you can copy after a failed run. In VS Code, Diagnose Workspace shows prerequisites and steps to fix them before a run.

The same distinction between an event and a record of it matters after release. Our release calendar can show individual versions by date because the source records contain release dates or commits. GitHub's asset download counter is a running total. When a day has no stored observation, the next reading tells us how much the counter moved over the interval.

Install Workbench 0.108.0 from the Visual Studio Marketplace.
